text: Lesson one ended with one clear sentence of a requirement. This lesson turns that sentence into a plan — the actual list of Snowflake objects this project needs, named and ordered, before a single one of them gets created.

Three of the six pieces come first. A warehouse, to run the load and the query — small, because this is one table and one summary, not a company-wide workload. A stage, which is just a landing spot for the daily ticket export, a CSV file, before it's loaded. And a raw table, holding one row per support ticket exactly as exported, no transformation applied yet.

The last three pieces turn that raw data into the actual answer. A summary query — the real thing the VP of Support asked for, ticket count grouped by day and by priority. A view, wrapping that query so Power BI connects to one stable object instead of a raw query every time. And one role: a read-only analyst who can see that view, and nothing else.

Driftwood's data team already has a database for billing and usage data in the Advanced capstone, called Driftwood Analytics. There's no reason to spin up a second database for one more data domain, so this project adds its own schema, called Support, inside that same database. Five names, written down now, mean nobody improvises object names later in the build.

Notice what's deliberately missing from this plan. No dbt transformation layer — one create view statement is enough for one summary query. No orchestrator triggering the load — a person runs copy into by hand, for now; real automation with Streams and Tasks shows up in the Intermediate project. And no second role, because there's only one stakeholder so far.

That's the plan: six objects, named, in order. Next lesson, we build the first two pieces for real — creating the actual warehouse, and loading the ticket data into Snowflake with a real stage and a real COPY INTO statement.
